title: Urinary Bladder Pathology
subject: Pathology
summary: The bladder is a dynamic organ lined by urothelium; pathology ranges from infection to malignancy. Clinicians must link history, exam, and simple tests to distinguish common tropical infections, reflux, and cancers.

sections.p: The urinary bladder is a compliant reservoir lined by transitional epithelium. Diagnosis of bladder disease relies on history, physical signs, urine microscopy, and imaging when available.

t.b: Detects haematuria, leukocytes, nitrites – suggests infection or bleeding
Pyuria, haematuria, casts – indicates infection, inflammation or tumour
Shows wall thickening, masses, stones, hydronephrosis – first imaging in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Bladder cancers are staged by the TNM system; infections are graded by severity of haematuria and systemic signs.
In East Africa, schistosomiasis, urinary tract infections, and reflux dominate; later, smoking and schistosomiasis lead to carcinoma.
b: Schistosoma haematobium – eggs in bladder veins cause fibrosis and squamous metaplasia
E. coli – most common cystitis pathogen
Vesicoureteral reflux – predisposes to pyelonephritis and scarring

sections.p: Patients may report dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, painless haematuria, or obstructive symptoms. Chronic pain without infection suggests interstitial cystitis.
b: Painless haematuria – think tumour or schistosomiasis

sections.p: Start with simple urine tests; imaging if available; cystoscopy is definitive but often unavailable.

t.b: Detects bladder wall thickening, masses, stones, hydronephrosis
Direct visualisation of mucosa, biopsies for definitive diagnosis

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for massive haematuria, sepsis, bladder outlet obstruction, or suspected tumour.
b: Massive haematuria – possible tumour or severe infection

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and plan definitive treatment. Drug choice reflects local resistance patterns and drug availability.
b: Antibiotics – nitrofurantoin or ciprofloxacin for cystitis; avoid fluoroquinolones if resistance high
Tamsulosin – for bladder outlet obstruction in men

sections.p: Regular review for recurrent infections, monitor haematuria, and counsel on smoking cessation. Vaccinate against hepatitis B and treat schistosomiasis where endemic.
Urinary retention, prostate enlargement, and pelvic inflammatory disease can mimic bladder pathology.
b: Prostatitis – lower abdominal pain, dysuria, but normal bladder capacity

sections.p: Low‑grade tumours may show normal ultrasound; schistosomiasis can mimic infection on dipstick.
b: Normal ultrasound does not rule out early carcinoma

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with painless haematuria and a history of swimming in a lake – what is the most likely diagnosis? — Schistosoma haematobium infection; look for eggs on urine microscopy. A patient with recurrent cystitis and a history of smoking develops a mass on ultrasound – what is the next step? — Cystoscopy with biopsy to rule out urothelial carcinoma.
